analysis.one_liner: Shields hospitals and doctors from most lawsuits over care given during the COVID-19 emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Judiciary Committee from May 2020 until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred lawsuits against doctors, nurses, hospitals, nursing homes, clinics, and other health care entities for harm caused while arranging or providing care during the COVID-19 emergency, and for 60 days after it ended. It covered not just COVID treatment but any care given to any patient who showed up during the emergency. Only willful misconduct, gross negligence, recklessness, or practicing while intoxicated could still be sued over. It died without any action in the House Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospitals, nursing homes, medical clinics, group practices, and the doctors and staff who work in them would gain near-complete protection from malpractice suits for ordinary mistakes made during the pandemic — including harm tied to understaffing or a shortage of resources, and including care given to patients who did not have COVID at all. Medical malpractice insurers would also benefit, since fewer claims mean fewer payouts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hospitals, nursing homes, and malpractice insurers

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars liability 'under any law of the United States or of any State' for harm caused by an act or omission in the course of providing health care during the emergency period, as long as the provider acted in good faith or withheld care for pandemic-related reasons [S3].

The shield extends to acts taken based on any federal, state, or local official's guidance, or 'due to a lack of resources, including manpower, attributable to the COVID-19 pandemic' — meaning short-staffed care could still be protected [S3].
'Related health care entity' explicitly includes skilled nursing facilities, hospitals, academic medical centers, ambulatory surgical centers, group medical practices, and medical clinics [S3].
The protections would apply during the emergency period and for 60 days after it ends, and would preempt state laws that are inconsistent with the federal shield [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients harmed by negligent care during the pandemic — including people treated for conditions unrelated to COVID — would lose the ability to recover for ordinary malpractice, since the shield covers physical, nonphysical, economic, and noneconomic losses and only gross negligence or worse remains suable. State governments would also lose some say, since the federal shield preempts conflicting state law.

drawbacks.text: The shield covers every patient who presented for care during the emergency, not only COVID patients, and it applies to harm from care provided or withheld because of any official's guidance or a resource shortage — which could protect understaffed nursing homes from suits over neglect [S3].

Ordinary negligence — a standard malpractice mistake — would no longer be actionable; patients could only sue for willful or criminal misconduct, gross negligence, reckless misconduct, conscious flagrant indifference, or care provided while impaired [S3].
The bill does not say when the emergency period ends, and it adds 60 days of coverage after termination, leaving the duration of the shield open-ended at the time [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Providers did face real uncertainty in 2020 — shifting federal guidance, stretched staffing, and, for some clinicians, work far outside their usual practice. A narrow shield covering pandemic-specific care under official guidance would have answered that. This bill went much further: it covered all care for all patients during the emergency, protected harm caused by resource shortfalls, and preempted state law. The cost fell entirely on patients harmed by ordinary negligence, who would have had no remedy. A broader, longer shield than the problem called for.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Roe (R-TN) introduced the bill on May 28, 2020, joined by Rep. Lou Correa (D-CA), and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1][S5].
The bill attracted 38 cosponsors — 32 Republicans and 6 Democrats — but the House Judiciary Committee took no further action on it for the rest of the 116th Congress [S4][S5].
The bill never received a committee vote, never reached the House floor, and expired on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients harmed by negligent care kept their right to sue, since no federal liability shield became law — though many states enacted their own provider liability protections during 2020, so the practical gain was smaller than it looks. Hospitals and nursing homes avoided a federal preemption of state law but were not worse off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients who kept their right to sue

for.name: Rep. David P. Roe

for.name: Rep. Lou Correa
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as the Democratic co-lead [S3].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 28, 2020 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The lead pair was bipartisan (Roe, R-TN, with Correa, D-CA), but 32 of the 38 cosponsors were Republicans, and 6 of 231 House Democrats signed on.

industries.note: The bill would have barred nearly all malpractice suits against them for care during the emergency, including harm from resource shortfalls. Their gain was patients' loss of recourse, including for patients treated for conditions unrelated to COVID.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and skilled nursing facilities
industries.note: Explicitly named as covered entities, and the shield for harm 'due to a lack of resources, including manpower' could have protected understaffed facilities from suits over neglect during a period when they saw severe outbreaks.

industries.industry: Physicians and other health care professionals
industries.note: Individual clinicians would have gained protection for pandemic-era care outside their normal practice, which addressed a genuine worry for workers deployed to unfamiliar settings. The tradeoff is that patients injured by their ordinary mistakes could not recover.
A broad federal bar on claims would sharply cut payouts on policies written for hospitals and long-term care providers, keeping premium savings with the industry rather than patients.
